pair.title: Where "down" points
pair.mini: On a globe every vertical is a radius, so no two plumb lines are parallel. On a flat Earth, at its strongest, every vertical is parallel and every bubble level agrees. The two can be told apart with a plumb line and the stars.
pair.text: Where "down" points, in each model. On the globe every vertical is a radius, so no two plumb lines anywhere are parallel. On an infinite flat slab, the flat model at its strongest for this measurement, every vertical is perpendicular to the ground and parallel to every other, and every bubble level is centred. "Water finds its level" is true in both; the question is what level means. Geodesy defines it as the surface on which gravity does no work, and measures it [1]. The directions in the drawing are exact; the heights of the plumb bobs are schematic.
pair.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: plumb lines in distant places measured parallel against the stars.
angle.title: Two verticals meet at the centre
angle.mini: Extend two plumb lines a distance d apart downward: they meet at the Earth's centre, at an angle d/R. That is 1° for every 111.2 km, and astronomers measure it as a difference in latitude.
angle.text: Take two verticals a measured distance d apart along the ground and extend them downward. On a sphere they meet at the centre, and the angle between them is d/R: 1° for every 111.2 km. On a plane they never meet: the angle is zero at any distance. The direction of a plumb line can be compared with the stars, and that comparison is exactly what astronomic latitude is. So two observatories a known distance apart on one meridian measure the angle between their verticals directly. The drawing is schematic.
angle.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: plumb lines far apart that point in the same direction against the stars.
vglobe.title: Six plumb lines on the globe
vglobe.mini: Six plumb lines and six bubble levels around the globe, each perpendicular to its own radius. No two point the same way, yet every level is level where it stands.
vglobe.text: Six plumb lines and six bubble levels placed around the globe, each perpendicular to its own radius. No two plumb lines are parallel, yet every level is perfectly level where it stands, and water in every basin is flat at its own scale. This is what a round Earth means for gravity: down is a direction toward the centre, and it is a different direction everywhere. The difference between two places is the angle between them at the centre. The directions are exact; the observers' heights are schematic.
vglobe.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: verticals in distant places measured parallel.
vflat.title: Flat, at its strongest: an infinite slab
vflat.mini: For every vertical to be parallel and every level true, a flat Earth needs an infinite slab: no rim, no edge, infinite mass. A disc with a rim cannot do it.
vflat.text: The flat model at its strongest. For every plumb line to hang perpendicular to the ground and every bubble to be centred, the pull must be perpendicular to the surface everywhere, and only an infinite slab gives that: no rim, no ice wall, no edge, and infinite mass. A disc of finite size with a rim cannot hold every vertical perpendicular: toward its edge, its own mass pulls sideways. The drawing is schematic.
vflat.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: gravity measured perpendicular to the ground everywhere, with parallel plumb lines far apart.
verticals.title: Down is not the same direction twice
verticals.mini: On a globe, plumb lines point to the centre and none are parallel. On a flat Earth they would all be parallel. Compare a plumb line with the stars in two places and the angle between them is the distance over the radius.
verticals.text: On the globe, six plumb lines point toward the centre, each perpendicular to its own radius: no two are parallel, yet every level is level where it stands. On a flat Earth, at its strongest, an infinite slab would hold every vertical parallel and every bubble centred. The two predictions differ in a measurable way: the angle between the verticals of two places is d/R on a globe, 1° per 111.2 km, and zero on a plane. Comparing the plumb line with the stars measures it; geodesists have done it for centuries, and define level from the measured field [1]. Directions are exact; heights are schematic.
verticals.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: plumb lines in distant places pointing in the same direction against the stars.
slab.title: The best gravity a flat Earth can have
slab.mini: To pull at 9.8 m/s² everywhere and straight down, a flat Earth needs a fixed mass under every square metre, spread out with no edge anywhere: an infinite slab.
slab.text: Give the flat model the best gravity it can have. To pull at 9.8 m/s² straight down at every point, it needs the same mass under every square metre, spread out to infinity with no edge anywhere: an infinite slab. Its gravity would then be the same at every height, since an infinite plane's pull does not weaken with distance. At the Earth's mean density of 5,514 kg/m³ [1], the slab would need a definite thickness, but no size limit at all. Any map with a rim breaks this. The drawing is schematic.
slab.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: gravity that does not weaken with height, and verticals parallel everywhere.
disc.title: A disc with a rim tilts every level
disc.mini: Give the flat map a rim at 20,000 km and Earth's density, and compute its gravity. Down tilts toward the centre: about 7° at the latitude of Paris, 26° at the latitude of Sydney. A level is level only at the centre.
disc.text: The flat map needs a rim, about 20,000 km from the North Pole. Give that disc the Earth's mean density [1] and compute its gravity by integrating its own mass. The pull tilts toward the centre, zero at exactly one point, the centre, and growing outward: about 7° at the latitude of Paris and 26° at the latitude of Sydney. A 7° slope is a 12% grade. Rivers would all run north, seas would pile up toward the pole, and a bubble level would be visibly off in every building in Europe. No one on either side of the argument measures that.
disc.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: levels and plumb lines tilted toward the North Pole by several degrees across Europe.
gradient.title: Gravity weakens as you climb, and the rate is the radius
gradient.mini: On a globe gravity falls with height as g·R²/(R + h)². The rate, 0.3086 mGal per metre, applied in every gravity survey, inverts to give the Earth's radius: about 6,356 km.
gradient.text: On a globe, gravity weakens with height as g·R²/(R + h)², so near the ground it falls by 2g/R per metre. Read it the other way and it becomes an instrument: every gravity survey on Earth applies the free-air correction of 0.3086 mGal per metre before anything else [1], and that constant, inverted, gives R = 2g/0.3086 mGal/m, about 6,356 km, within a fraction of a percent of the Earth's mean radius. On an infinite slab, gravity does not change with height at all. The drawing is schematic.
gradient.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: gravity that stays the same as you climb.
grad.title: Measured loss of gravity with height
grad.mini: Gravity against height at true scale: a globe loses 0.3086 mGal per metre; an infinite slab loses nothing. A field gravimeter resolves 0.01 mGal, so the difference shows between two floors of a building.
grad.text: Gravity against height, at true scale. The teal curve is a globe's, g·R²/(R + h)²; the amber line is an infinite slab's, which does not change with height at all. The globe's rate, 0.3086 mGal per metre, is applied in every survey [1]. A field gravimeter resolves 0.01 mGal, so the difference between the pavement and the first floor of a building is dozens of times the noise. The fall has been mapped up a real hillside with a portable atom interferometer [2], and airborne surveys apply it at 11 km [3].
grad.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: gravity unchanged between the ground and the top of a building or a hill.
lat.title: Gravity changes with latitude: Richer's clock, 1672
lat.mini: In 1672 Jean Richer's pendulum clock, exact in Paris, ran 2 min 28 s a day slow at Cayenne, near the equator. Gravity is weaker there. Every flat model predicts one value everywhere.
lat.text: Jean Richer took a pendulum clock to Cayenne, 5° from the equator, and found it running 2 min 28 s a day slow against the stars, after keeping perfect time in Paris [1]. A pendulum's period depends only on its length and on g, so the clock was a gravimeter: gravity is weaker near the equator. The teal curve is the modern reference formula fitted to worldwide gravimetry [2]; the dashed curve is what rotation alone would do to a sphere, about two thirds of the observed spread, the rest coming from the equatorial bulge. The amber line is every flat model, with one value everywhere. The black dot is Richer's clock, the only observation plotted.
lat.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the same gravity at every latitude, and pendulum clocks that keep the same rate everywhere.
tide.title: Why two tides a day
tide.mini: The whole Earth falls towards the Moon. What is left of the Moon's pull once the centre's is taken away stretches the oceans into two bulges, one under the Moon and one opposite. The Earth turns under them: two high waters every 24 h 50 min.
tide.text: Most coasts have two high waters a day, 12 h 25 min apart, and the second comes when the Moon is on the other side of the Earth. The whole Earth falls towards the Moon with the pull its centre feels; the near side is pulled harder than that, the far side less hard, so both bulge outward by the same amount, 2GMr/d³. The Earth turns under the two bulges once every 24 h 50 min. Kepler's third law, GM/d³ = (2π/T)², gives the Sun's share from the month, the year and the masses alone: 0.46 of the Moon's, hence spring tides at new and full moon and neap tides at the quarters, every 14.77 days. On a plane every point is on the same side of the Moon: one hump, one tide a day. The water heights are drawn millions of times higher than they are, and the factor is written on each picture.
tide.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: one high water per lunar day, under the Moon, and no twice-daily tide anywhere.
gauges.title: Five tide gauges, one year
gauges.mini: A year of hourly sea level at Brest, Marseille, Pensacola, Manila and Fremantle. Every record has its lines at the Moon's and Sun's frequencies; the twice-daily one is at 12.421 h at all five, and the daily range beats at 14.77 or 13.66 days.
gauges.text: A reading every hour for all of 2018 at five gauges of the University of Hawaii Sea Level Center, chosen for their differences: Brest big and twice daily, Marseille almost none, Pensacola once a day, Manila mixed, Fremantle small and daily. Read with the gauge's clock alone, the strongest twice-daily line is at 12.421 h everywhere, the Moon's half-day; the daily range swells and shrinks every 14.77 days where the twice-daily tide leads, the Moon's and Sun's bulges in and out of step, and every 13.66 days where the daily tide leads, the Moon's declination. The heights depend on each basin: Brest's Sun/Moon ratio is 0.36, not the 0.46 of Kepler, while the Moon's ellipse line N2 keeps its 0.19. Bottom: March 2018, with the Moon's phases and declination.
gauges.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a coast with no line at 12 h 25 min, or spring tides that do not follow the Moon's phases.
tglobe.title: The pull and the real tides on one globe
tglobe.mini: The surface the Moon and the Sun would give a still ocean, and the tide 613 gauges actually measure, at the same instant and scale. Same clock everywhere; each coast early or late.
tglobe.text: A turning Earth seen from 90° to the Moon. Shading and outline: the equilibrium tide, the surface the Moon's and the Sun's pull would give a still ocean, from their true positions. Spikes: 613 tide gauges of TICON-3, each showing the tide its own measured constants give for that instant, at the same scale. The spikes rise and fall with the bulges' clock, twice a day, more at new and full moon, but not under the bulges: each ocean basin answers the pull with its own delays and has points where the tide vanishes. Three scenes: two days from the new moon of 17 March 2018; the Moon's M2 line alone; a month seen once every lunar day, where only spring and neap remain. Heights are drawn 9 × 10⁵ times higher, the same for surface and spikes.
tglobe.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: gauges whose tides follow no twice-daily clock, or no spring-neap cycle tied to the Moon's phases.
seas.title: Why small seas have almost no tide
seas.mini: A closed basin can only tilt under the pull: at most A·L/R, a few centimetres for a sea 1,000 km long. Measured: Atlantic Europe 1.3 m, Mediterranean 7 cm, Black Sea 2 cm, Baltic under 1 cm; Fundy 3.3 m by resonance.
seas.text: Over the open ocean the bulges travel round the Earth and the water is carried in from far away. A closed lake cannot be fed: the pull only tilts its surface, by at most A·L/R, with A = 0.24 m and L its length. Lake Geneva: 3 mm at most; Lake Superior: 2 cm, and the NOAA gives under 5 cm for its spring tide; the Black Sea: 4 cm at most, 2 cm measured. The M2 tide at TICON-3's gauges: 1.3 m on the Atlantic coast of Europe, 7 cm in the Mediterranean (Gibraltar lets a little in), 2 cm in the Black Sea, under 1 cm in the Baltic. A bay open at one end with a natural period 4L/√(gh) near 12 h 25 min rings: the Bay of Fundy reaches several metres. A Moon lifting water under itself would lift lakes as much as oceans.
seas.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a closed lake with a tide as large as the open coast nearby.
